title: The smoke
hookLine: watch for the day the sky brings a visible smoke (44:10)
last: A NIGHT BETTER THAN A THOUSAND MONTHS.

lines: SMOKE BETWEEN HIM AND THE SKY.
cards: A man in a starving city looks up, and between him and the sky he sees something like smoke. Hold that picture; it comes from an early report.
Surah Ad-Dukhan takes its name from one word in its tenth verse: dukhan, smoke. And the companions of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ did not agree about what that smoke was.
One of them thought it had already happened, in a hungry time in Mecca. Others thought it was still coming.

teach.b: Here is the verse in plain words: watch for the day when the sky brings a smoke plain to see. The next verse says it will cover the people, a painful torment, and they cry out to their Lord to remove it.

Then it will be lifted for a little while, and they will return to their ways. Two readings come down from the earliest generation. The first is from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari.

teach.h: IBN MAS'UD: A FAMINE IN MECCA.
teach.b: The Quraysh of Mecca resisted the Prophet so hard that he prayed against them, and a famine came, until people ate bones and carrion.

A man would look up at the sky and see something like smoke between himself and it, from the hunger. Then the Meccans asked for relief, it came, and they went back to what they had been doing, just as the verses describe.
For Ibn Mas'ud, the smoke was a past event. The second reading, linked to 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas, says the smoke is one of the great signs before the Last Day.

teach.h: OTHERS: A SIGN BEFORE THE HOUR.
teach.b: A hadith in Sahih Muslim lists ten signs before the Hour, and the smoke is among them. Some scholars hold both: a smoke that came, and a smoke still to come. In every reading, the shape stays the same.
Something in the sky makes people afraid. They cry out. Relief comes.

teach.h: THEY ASK, IT LIFTS, THEY FORGET.
teach.b: And then, very quickly, they forget they ever asked. The surah isn't only describing a catastrophe. It's describing how short human memory can be once the air clears.

how: Muslims read Ad-Dukhan as part of the Qur'an's warnings; commentators teach both readings of the smoke, the famine in Mecca and a sign before the Last Day.

o: dukhan, a sign in the sky, past or still to come
fumes rising from hellfire on the Last Day
incense burned in the mosque on Fridays

games.q: two readings of the smoke — tap the pairs.

s: the companions all agreed on what the smoke was
Ibn Mas'ud saw it as a past famine; others as a sign before the Hour.
in the verses, the relief is followed by forgetting
the smoke lifts for a while, and the people return to their ways.
the surah is named after a word in its tenth verse

games.q: you're a Meccan in the famine years. the sky looks like smoke. what does the surah say people do?
o: they cry out for relief, then forget once it comes.
games.why: the verses describe people asking for the torment to be lifted, and returning to their ways when it is.

practice: Breathe in through the nose and feel how cool the air is on the way in, how warm on the way out; you didn't earn it, and you didn't ask for it this morning.
Think of a day the air was bad, smoke from a fire, a stuffy room, a cold that blocked everything, then come back to this breath, clear. If you pray, you can say alhamdulillah for the air itself.

wordCard.voice: The smoke. Dukhan: the sign in 44:10, read by Ibn Mas'ud as a famine haze in Mecca, and by others as a sign still to come. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: smoke; the word that names surah 44.

carryVoice: Your line: a sign in the sky. Relief comes quickly, and so does forgetting. Day five hundred seventy-three, done.
